Consider a directed weighted graph G(V, E), where V is the set of vertices and E is the set of edges. Suppose we use adjacency list to implement the graph. Consider a sequence of |V| operations with each corresponding to a different vertex in V. For the operation for vertex v, the cost is assumed to be the number of outgoing edges from v.  (a) What is the cost of the worst possible single operation in this sequence of operations? (b) What is the average amortized cost of the above sequence of operations based on aggregate analysis?

message.content:
The worst possible single operation occurs when a vertex has the maximum possible number of outgoing edges, which in a directed graph with |V| vertices (assuming no self-loops) is |V| - 1. Using aggregate analysis, the total cost across all |V| operations equals the total number of edges |E|, since every directed edge contributes exactly one unit to the out-degree of its unique source vertex.

* (a) The cost of the worst possible single operation is **|V| - 1**. This is achieved when some vertex v has an outgoing edge to every other vertex in the graph, giving it an out-degree of |V| - 1.

* (b) The average amortized cost of the sequence of operations is **|E| / |V|**. This is derived by aggregate analysis: the total (aggregate) cost of all |V| operations is the sum of the out-degrees of all vertices, which equals |E|; dividing this total by the number of operations |V| yields the amortized cost of |E| / |V| per operation.
